extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and researchers of media studies, internet culture, and memetics
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic framework and research directions for studying Internet memes, including definitions, distinctions (form/content/stance; virality vs memetic uptake), platform roles, localization effects, and methodological recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, content, and stance distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividing memes to form, content and stance may be useful in understanding mechanisms of localization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format (the template) can be copied across cultures while content and satirical stance are altered; this may change the meme's meaning. Example: Israeli versions copied the American 'Successful Black Man' format but changed content and stance (tagging a name turned the character into a singular exception, thereby undermining the original's satirical critique). Use the threefold division to analyze what was preserved versus what was transformed in local adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet meme (three-part operational definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) A group of digital content units sharing common characteristics of content, form, and/or stance; (b) units are created with awareness of each other; (c) these units are circulated, imitated, and/or transformed via the Internet by many users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use all three criteria to identify a meme: shared template/topic/stance, intertextual awareness among producers, and multi-user circulation/remix. Example: photos of cats with captions share topic (cats), form (photo+caption), and stance (humor), and are circulated and remixed by many users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virality versus memetic success
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms 'viral' and 'memetic' are not coextensive: viral success refers to probability an item will be shared; memetic success refers to probability people will respond creatively by remaking or remixing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different features drive sharing versus creative uptake; researchers and practitioners should distinguish objectives (maximize shares vs maximize derivatives). For measurement, viral success emphasizes speed and reach metrics; memetic success emphasizes the volume and diversity of user-generated derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features that enhance memetic appeal (simplicity, repetition, whimsical/puzzling content)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of simple, repetitive elements and content that appears whimsical or puzzling encourages imitation and allows incorporation of a wide arena of themes into derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Gangnam Style' uses repetitive dance moves and whimsical puzzling imagery, enabling easy imitation (horse dance, recurring expressions) while allowing diverse thematic substitutions (national, political, institutional, personal). When evaluating or designing potentially memetic media, assess template simplicity and openness for reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity circles of meme adaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: Adaptations of a meme tend to relate to four distinct identity circles: (1) national/regional/subcultural identity; (2) social satire/political commentary; (3) institutional self-promotion; (4) personal/ceremonial personalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to classify derivatives and interpret intent. Examples: (1) 'Orang Sabah Style' (tourism outward-facing) or internal subcultural jokes in Saudi versions; (2) 'Mitt Romney Style' as political satire; (3) 'NASA Johnson Style' as institutional promotion; (4) wedding/bar mitzvah remakes as personal/ceremonial versions that use vernacular locations and participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization may alter satirical stance and stereotype dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Local adaptations that alter content or add identifiers (e.g., naming a character) can convert a meme's general satirical inversion into an exception that validates existing stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing localized versions, check whether changes preserve subversive stance or instead present a single exceptional figure (which may reinforce stereotypes). Example: tagging a Haredi character by name in an Israeli adaptation makes the humanistic trait appear limited to a single exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politics of memetic participation (participant demographics & power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes are produced and diffused by people; understanding who participates and how participation patterns relate to race, ethnicity, gender, and power is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess representation among creators and presenters (e.g., Noam Gal's study showed 'It Gets Better' presenters were mostly white young males). Use case studies to evaluate whether memes provide alternative voices for marginalized groups or reproduce entrenched power structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes as a language and cultural capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes constitute a secondary layer of language whose correct use requires familiarity with subcultural standards; appropriate or 'inappropriate' usage is negotiated within meme hubs and can function as cultural capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate meme use by considering audience knowledge and hub-specific norms (e.g., 4chan practices). Incorrect or outsider usage signals lack of community membership; mastery of meme conventions can confer status within a community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring a meme's 'effect' versus its diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond counts of shares or views, research should probe what constitutes an Internet meme's 'effect' (e.g., political influence, legislative change) and develop measures for that effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between visibility metrics (virality) and substantive outcomes (political or cultural influence). Use mixed methods to trace causal pathways from memetic activity to offline consequences; acknowledge that high memetic visibility does not automatically produce policy or regime change (e.g., Occupy Wall Street case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative dynamics: mutual reinforcement of originals and remixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Each derivative strengthens the status of the original viral video, while the initial viral video helps promote its derivatives; memetic videos thus compete well in attention economies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating memetic ecosystems, consider the feedback loop where remixes amplify the original and the original legitimizes remixes. This has practical implications for advertisers and campaigners aiming to build 'memetic' franchises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform-specific characteristics of prevalent meme hubs
rubrics_metrics.description: Different platforms (4chan, Tumblr, Reddit) have distinct structural and cultural features that shape meme creation and diffusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 4chan: imageboard divided into boards, anonymity, /b/ 'random' board with aggressive style; important hub for meme origin and hacktivist culture. Tumblr: microblogging/tumblogs and following model, image-rich posts, supports circulation of visual memes. Reddit: link aggregation with up/down voting, subreddits for topics, community moderation; characterized as 'lefty' or 'geeky' hub. Use platform affordances and norms when analyzing meme behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological recommendation: combine quantitative big-data and qualitative close reading; attend to genre-specific factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensive understanding of memes requires both large-scale quantitative analysis and qualitative close readings, as well as comparative cross-cultural studies and attention to genre-specific factors that affect memetic uptake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on an overarching general model; investigate nuanced, genre- and context-specific drivers of virality and mimesis (e.g., advertising vs political campaigns). Employ mixed methods to capture diffusion patterns, creative practices, and cultural meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of virality (operational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virality is a diffusion process in which a message spreads rapidly and broadly by bridging multiple networks; viral content is often defined by speed and broad reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize virality with metrics of temporal growth (speed), reach (number/diversity of networks reached), and bridging across communities. Note: when viral content generates user-created derivatives it may also be memetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/memetic definition (Dawkins' meme concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes (Dawkins): small cultural units of transmission spread by copying or imitation, analogous to genes; they undergo variation, competition, selection, and retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this conceptual framing to analyze memes as replicators subject to selective pressures in sociocultural environments. Recognize the distinction between this theoretical origin and contemporary operational definitions of Internet memes.
